t.3.40.1: Having thus spoken harsh words to Rāvaṇa, Mārīca, dejected and afraid of the lord of the night-wanderers, then said, "Let us both go."
t.3.40.2: And again I was seen by him, bearing arrows, bow and sword, his weapon raised to slay me, and my life was as good as destroyed.
t.3.40.3: But what can I do, when you are so wicked-minded? Here I go, dear one; may it be well with you, O night-wanderer.
t.3.40.4: That rākṣasa was overjoyed at those words, and, embracing him closely, he spoke these words.
t.3.40.5: This speech of yours, full of valour, is spoken as if in accordance with my own wish. Now you are Mārīca; before, you were some other night-roamer.
t.3.40.6: Let this sky-going chariot, adorned with jewels and yoked with asses that have the faces of piśācas, be mounted quickly together with me.
t.3.40.7: Then Rāvaṇa and Mārīca mounted that chariot, which was like a celestial vimāna, and swiftly departed from that circle of hermitages.
t.3.40.8: Just so, the two of them, looking there upon towns and forests, mountains and all the rivers, kingdoms and cities alike,
t.3.40.9: Then, having reached the Daṇḍaka forest, Rāvaṇa, lord of the Rākṣasas, together with Mārīca, beheld the hermitage of Rāghava.
t.3.40.10: Then, having descended from that chariot adorned with gold, Rāvaṇa took Mārīca by the hand and spoke these words.
t.3.40.11: This is the site of Rāma's hermitage, seen surrounded by plantain trees. Friend, let that be done quickly for the sake of which we have come.
t.3.40.12: Then the rākṣasa Mārīca, having heard Rāvaṇa's words, became a deer and roamed about at the entrance of Rāma's hermitage.
t.3.40.13: He had horn-tips of the choicest gems and a face shaped in white and dark. His mouth was like a red lotus and water-lily, and his ears were like water-lilies of sapphire.
t.3.40.14: With its neck slightly raised, its belly gleaming like sapphire and its flanks like madhūka flowers, it shone with the hue of lotus filaments.
t.3.40.15: His hooves gleamed like beryl, his legs were slender, his body compact and well-knit, and he shone with his tail held high, bright with the hues of Indra's bow.
t.3.40.16: In an instant the rākṣasa became a deer of surpassing beauty, its hue charming and lustrous, covered with gems of many kinds.
t.3.40.17: Having assumed a form that was enchanting and lovely to behold, that rākṣasa set aglow the delightful forest and that site of Rāma's hermitage.
t.3.40.18: To allure Vaidehī, he took a form variegated with many mineral hues, and, wandering about, he moves freely over the grassy meadows on every side.
t.3.40.19: Dappled with hundreds of silver spots and lovely to behold, he wandered about, breaking off the tender shoots of the trees and eating them.
t.3.40.20: Going to the little bower of plantains, moving with a slow gait, he then took shelter here and there among the karṇikāra trees, so as to come within Sītā's sight.
t.3.40.21: That great deer, its back dappled as if with lotuses, shone splendidly, and it roamed at its ease near Rāma's hermitage.
t.3.40.22: Going off again and turning back, that finest of deer roamed about; having gone swiftly for a moment, it returns once more.
t.3.40.23: Frolicking about, he would sit down again and again upon the ground; then, coming up to the door of the hermitage, he would go off toward the herds of deer.
t.3.40.24: Followed by herds of deer, the rākṣasa who had taken on the form of a deer kept turning back again, longing for a sight of Sītā.
t.3.40.25: Darting forth, he roams about in wondrous circles; and all the other deer that range the forest, having gazed upon him...
t.3.40.26: Approaching him and sniffing, they flee in all ten directions; and that rākṣasa too, though he delighted in the slaughter of deer, spared those forest deer.
t.3.40.28: Absorbed in gathering flowers, the lady with intoxicating eyes moved on past the trees, past the karṇikāras, the aśokas and the mango trees.
t.3.40.27: To conceal his true nature, he only touched the plants but did not eat them. Then, at that very moment, Vaidehī of the lovely eyes…
t.3.40.29: The fair-faced lady was wandering about, gathering flowers. That most excellent of women, who did not deserve a life of dwelling in the forest, saw that deer made of jewels, its body dappled with pearls and gems.
t.3.40.31: And that illusory deer, gazing at her, the beloved of Rāma, then roamed about there, as if setting that forest aglow.
t.3.40.30: With eyes wide open in wonder, she gazed with affection at that deer, whose teeth and lips were lovely and whose hair shone with the hues of silver and mineral ores.
t.3.40.32: Seeing that deer, never seen before and made of many kinds of jewels, Sītā, the daughter of Janaka, was filled with the greatest wonder.
